title: How Much Does EU AI Act Compliance Cost in 2026? — A Deployer's Budgeting Guide
context: 2026-09-01 EAT cycle — answer-first seed covering the real costs of EU AI Act compliance for deployers: personnel, documentation, conformity assessment, and ongoing monitoring. Built from publicly reported figures, notified-body fee schedules, and Council of AI measurement economics.
body: The cost of EU AI Act compliance depends on what kind of AI system you deploy, but the short answer is: budget €15,000–€85,000 for a limited-risk system's first-year compliance and €120,000–€450,000+ for a high-risk system — and those are deployer-side costs, not provider-side. Here is the breakdown. First, classification cost (€2,000–€8,000): before you spend anything on compliance, you must determine whether your AI system is prohibited, high-risk, limited-risk, or minimal-risk under Article 6 and Annex III. This requires a documented legal analysis; most organisations spend 20–40 hours of counsel or specialist consultant time. Second, personnel (€60,000–€180,000/year for high-risk; €8,000–€25,000 for limited-risk): Article 4 mandates AI literacy for all staff operating the system, and high-risk deployers need someone performing the human oversight function under Article 14 — this is not a full-time role for most SMEs but it is a named accountability. Third, documentation (€10,000–€50,000 for high-risk; €3,000–€12,000 for limited-risk): high-risk systems require technical documentation under Article 11, record-keeping under Article 12, and transparency notifications under Article 13. A deployer using a provider's CE-marked system inherits much of the provider's documentation but must still produce its own deployment-context records. Fourth, conformity assessment (€8,000–€35,000 for self-assessment; €50,000–€200,000+ for notified-body involvement under Annex III): most deployers of off-the-shelf high-risk AI rely on the provider's CE mark and do not need a fresh notified-body assessment — but if you substantially modify the system, you become a provider and the cost jumps. Fifth, fundamental rights impact assessment or FRIA (€5,000–€25,000): Article 27 applies to bodies governed by public law and certain private deployers. Sixth, ongoing monitoring (€5,000–€30,000/year): Article 49 post-market monitoring, incident reporting under Article 62, and maintaining the EU database registration under Article 64. Council of AI verified measurement can reduce ongoing monitoring costs by producing auditable, signed measurement records that replace manual evidence-gathering — a typical deployer saves 40–60% of annual audit preparation costs by using a measurement credential rather than assembling documentation from scratch each cycle. For a limited-risk system (e.g., an AI chatbot with transparency labelling), the first-year cost is typically €15,000–€35,000 including documentation, AI literacy training, and transparency compliance. For a high-risk system in HR, education, or critical infrastructure, the first-year cost is €120,000–€350,000 for a deployer who does not modify the system, and €250,000–€450,000+ if you cross the line into provider status. The single most expensive mistake deployers make is blurring the deployer/provider boundary — that one determination can multiply your compliance budget by a factor of three to five. Get the classification right first.
